questions.q: If $I_n = \int\limits_0^{\pi/4}\tan^n x\ dx, n \in \mathbb{N}$ then $I_{n+2} + I_n$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$I_{n+2} + I_n = \int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \tan^{n+2} x\ dx + \int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \tan^n x\ dx$

$I_{n+2} + I_n = \int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \tan^n x (\tan^2 x + 1)\ dx$

$I_{n+2} + I_n = \int\limits_0^{\pi/4} \tan^n x \sec^2 x\ dx$

Substituting $t = \tan x$, we get $dt = \sec^2 x\ dx$.

When $x = 0$, $t = 0$ and when $x = \pi/4$, $t = 1$.

$I_{n+2} + I_n = \int\limits_0^1 t^n\ dt$

$I_{n+2} + I_n = \left[ \dfrac{t^{n+1}}{n+1} \right]_0^1$

$I_{n+2} + I_n = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{n + 1}$

questions.q: If $\int\limits_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(\sin^2 x + \sin^3 x)dx = k$, then the value of $k$
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sin^2 x + \sin^3 x) dx$

$I = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin^2 x dx + \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin^3 x dx$

Since $\sin^3 x$ is an odd function, $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin^3 x dx = 0$

Since $\sin^2 x$ is an even function, $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin^2 x dx = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^2 x dx$

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^2 x dx = 2 \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Therefore, $k = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.q: The value of the integral $\int\limits_{1/e}^{e}\dfrac{|\log x|}{x^2}dx$ is
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int\limits_{1/e}^{e}\dfrac{|\log x|}{x^2}dx$

Substitute $x = e^t \Rightarrow dx = e^t dt$

When $x = 1/e$, $t = -1$ and when $x = e$, $t = 1$

$I = \int\limits_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{|t|}{e^{2t}} e^t dt = \int\limits_{-1}^{1} |t| e^{-t} dt$

Splitting the integral at $t = 0$:

$I = \int\limits_{-1}^{0} -t e^{-t} dt + \int\limits_{0}^{1} t e^{-t} dt$

Using integration by parts:

$\int -t e^{-t} dt = t e^{-t} + e^{-t}$

$\int t e^{-t} dt = -t e^{-t} - e^{-t}$

Evaluating the definite integrals:

$I = \left[ t e^{-t} + e^{-t} \right]_{-1}^{0} + \left[ -t e^{-t} - e^{-t} \right]_{0}^{1}$

$I = \left( (0 + e⁰) - (-e¹ + e¹) \right) + \left( (-e^{-1} - e^{-1}) - (0 - e⁰) \right)$

$I = (1 - 0) + \left( -\dfrac{2}{e} - (-1) \right)$

$I = 1 + 1 - \dfrac{2}{e} =2 - \dfrac{2}{e}$

Answer: $2 - \dfrac{2}{e}$

questions.q: If $\int_0^1 \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x + 1} - \sqrt{x}} = \sqrt{2}k$, then the value of $k$ is...
questions.solution:
Rationalizing the denominator of the integrand:

$\int_0^1 \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x + 1} - \sqrt{x}} = \int_0^1 \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 1} + \sqrt{x}}{(\sqrt{x + 1})^2 - (\sqrt{x})^2} dx$

$= \int_0^1 (\sqrt{x + 1} + \sqrt{x}) dx$

Integrating with respect to $x$:

$= \left[ \dfrac{2}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2} + \dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2} \right]_0^1$

Applying the limits:

$= \left( \dfrac{2}{3}(2)^{3/2} + \dfrac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2} \right) - \left( \dfrac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2} + 0 \right)$

$= \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}$

$= \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}$

Equating to the given value $\sqrt{2}k$:

$\sqrt{2}k = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}$

$k = \dfrac{4}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{3}$

questions.q: If $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$, then the value of the integral $\int_0^2 x^2[x]\, dx$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The given integral is $I = \int_0^2 x^2[x]\, dx$.

Using the property of the greatest integer function, we split the integral at integer points within the limits of integration:

$I = \int_0^1 x^2[x]\, dx + \int_1^2 x^2[x]\, dx$

For $x \in [0, 1)$, $[x] = 0$.

For $x \in [1, 2)$, $[x] = 1$.

Substituting these values into the integrals:

$I = \int_0^1 x^2(0)\, dx + \int_1^2 x^2(1)\, dx$

$I = 0 + \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right]_1^2$

$I = \dfrac{2^3}{3} - \dfrac{1^3}{3}$

$I = \dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{7}{3}$

questions.q: The value of integral $\int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{1 + e^x}\,dx$ is...
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{1 + e^x} dx$

Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $e^{-x}$:

$I = \int_0^\infty \dfrac{e^{-x}}{e^{-x} + 1} dx$

Let $e^{-x} + 1 = t$

Differentiating both sides, $-e^{-x} dx = dt \Rightarrow e^{-x} dx = -dt$

Limits of integration:

When $x = 0$, $t = e^0 + 1 = 2$

When $x \to \infty$, $t = e^{-\infty} + 1 = 1$

Substituting these into the integral:

$I = \int_2^1 \dfrac{-dt}{t} = \int_1^2 \dfrac{dt}{t}$

$I = [\log t]_1^2 = \log 2 - \log 1 = \log 2$

Answer: $\log 2$

questions.q: If $f(x) = |5x - 3|$ is defined on interval $[0,1]$, then the value of $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$ is...
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_0^1 |5x - 3| \, dx$

The expression $5x - 3$ changes sign at $x = \dfrac{3}{5}$. Splitting the integral at this point:

$I = \int_0^{3/5} (3 - 5x) \, dx + \int_{3/5}^1 (5x - 3) \, dx$

$I = \left[ 3x - \dfrac{5x^2}{2} \right]_0^{3/5} + \left[ \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - 3x \right]_{3/5}^1$

$I = \left( 3\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) - \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right) \right) + \left( \left(\dfrac{5}{2} - 3\right) - \left(\dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right) -3\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\right) \right)

$I = $\left( \dfrac{9}{5} - \dfrac{9}{10} \right) + \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} -\left(\dfrac{9}{10} - \dfrac{9}{5}\right) \right)

$ I = $\dfrac{9}{10} + \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{9}{10} \right)

$ I = $\dfrac{9}{10} + \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{13}{10}$

Answer: $\dfrac{13}{10}$

questions.q: The value of $\displaystyle\int_2^4 (\{x\} + [x])\,dx =$...(where $\{x\}$ and $[x]$ are the fractional part function and the greatest integer function, respectively)
questions.solution:
By the definition of the fractional part and greatest integer functions, $x = [x] + \{x\}$.

Substituting this into the integral:

$\displaystyle\int_2^4 (\{x\} + [x])\,dx = \displaystyle\int_2^4 x\,dx$

Evaluating the definite integral:

$\displaystyle\int_2^4 x\,dx = \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_2^4$

$= \dfrac{16}{2} - \dfrac{4}{2}$

$= 8 - 2 = 6$

Answer: $6$

questions.q: If $[x]$ is the greatest integer function not greater than $x$, then the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x[x^2]\,dx$ is...
questions.solution:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int_0^2 x[x^2]\,dx$

Substitute $x^2 = t \Rightarrow 2x\,dx = dt \Rightarrow x\,dx = \dfrac{dt}{2}$

When $x = 0$, $t = 0$ and when $x = 2$, $t = 4$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \displaystyle\int_0^4 [t]\,dt$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \displaystyle\int_0^1 0\,dt + \displaystyle\int_1^2 1\,dt + \displaystyle\int_2^3 2\,dt + \displaystyle\int_3^4 3\,dt \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} (0 + 1(2-1) + 2(3-2) + 3(4-3))$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} (1 + 2 + 3) = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3$

Answer: $3$

Let $I = \int_0^2 x(2 - x)^b \, dx$.

Using the property $\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = \int_0^a f(a - x) \, dx$, we get:

$I = \int_0^2 (2 - x)(2 - (2 - x))^b \, dx$

$I = \int_0^2 (2 - x)x^b \, dx$

$I = \int_0^2 (2x^b - x^{b+1}) \, dx$

Integrating the terms, we get:

$I = \left[ \dfrac{2x^{b+1}}{b+1} - \dfrac{x^{b+2}}{b+2} \right]_0^2$

$I = \dfrac{2 \cdot 2^{b+1}}{b+1} - \dfrac{2^{b+2}}{b+2}$

$I = 2^{b+2} \left( \dfrac{1}{b+1} - \dfrac{1}{b+2} \right)

$I = $\dfrac{2^{b+2}}{(b+1)(b+2)}

It is given that $ I = $\dfrac{32}{7}.

\dfrac{2^{b+2}}{(b+1)(b+2)} = \dfrac{32}{7}

Substituting $ b = 6$ from the options:

\dfrac{2^{6+2}}{(6+1)(6+2)} = \dfrac{2^8}{7 \times 8} = \dfrac{256}{56} = \dfrac{32}{7}

This satisfies the given equation. Therefore, $ b = 6$.

Answer: 6$

questions.q: If $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function, then $\int_0^{\pi/3}[\tan x]\,dx = $
questions.solution:
The given integral is $I = \int_0^{\pi/3} [\tan x] \, dx$.

In the interval $[0, \pi/3]$, the function $\tan x$ is strictly increasing.

For $0 \le x < \pi/4$, $0 \le \tan x < 1 \Rightarrow [\tan x] = 0$.

For $\pi/4 \le x \le \pi/3$, $1 \le \tan x \le \sqrt{3} < 2 \Rightarrow [\tan x] = 1$.

Splitting the integral at $x = \pi/4$, we get:

$I = \int_0^{\pi/4} 0 \, dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3} 1 \, dx$

$I = 0 + [x]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}$

$I = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$

questions.q: The value of the definite integral $\int_0^{\log_e 5}\dfrac{e^x\sqrt{e^x-1}}{e^x+3}\,dx$ is equal to...
questions.solution:
Let $e^x - 1 = t^2$, which gives $e^x dx = 2t dt$.

When $x = 0$, $t = 0$.

When $x = \log_e 5$, $t = 2$.

The integral becomes:

$I = \int_0^2 \dfrac{t}{t^2 + 1 + 3} (2t dt) = \int_0^2 \dfrac{2t^2}{t^2 + 4} dt$

$I = 2 \int_0^2 \dfrac{t^2 + 4 - 4}{t^2 + 4} dt$

$I = 2 \int_0^2 \left( 1 - \dfrac{4}{t^2 + 4} \right) dt$

$I = 2 \left[ t - 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} \left( \dfrac{t}{2} \right) \right]_0^2

$I = 2 $\left[2 - 2 \tan^{-1}(1) \right]

$I = 2 $\left(2 - 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)

$I = 4 - \pi

Answer: 4 - \pi

questions.q: Let $f(x) = x - [x]$ for every real number $x$, where $[x]$ is integral part of $x$. then $\int\limits_{-1}^{1} f(x)\, dx$ is
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = x - [x]$

The integral is $\int_{-1}^{1} (x - [x]) \, dx$

This can be separated as $\int_{-1}^{1} x \, dx - \int_{-1}^{1} [x] \, dx$

Since $x$ is an odd function, $\int_{-1}^{1} x \, dx = 0$

For the second integral, we split the limits at the integer value $0$:

$\int_{-1}^{1} [x] \, dx = \int_{-1}^{0} [x] \, dx + \int_{0}^{1} [x] \, dx$

In the interval $(-1,0)$, $[x] = -1$ and in the interval $(0,1)$, $[x] = 0$

$\int_{-1}^{1} [x] \, dx = \int_{-1}^{0} (-1) \, dx + \int_{0}^{1} 0 \, dx$

$= -1[x]_{-1}^{0} + 0$

$= -1(0 - (-1)) = -1$

Substituting these back, we get:

$\int_{-1}^{1} (x - [x]) \, dx = 0 - (-1) = 1$

Answer: $1$

questions.q: The value of the definite integral $\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{5 + 4\cos x}\, dx$ is equal to...
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{5 + 4\cos x}\, dx$

Using the half-angle substitution $\cos x = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2(x/2)}{1 + \tan^2(x/2)}$ and $dx = \dfrac{2\, dt}{1 + t^2}$ where $t = \tan(x/2)$

The limits change from $x = 0 \rightarrow \pi$ to $t = 0 \rightarrow \infty$

$I = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{5 + 4\left(\dfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}\right)} \dfrac{2\, dt}{1 + t^2}$

$I = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2\, dt}{5(1 + t^2) + 4(1 - t^2)}$

$I = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2\, dt}{9 + t^2}$

$I = 2 \left[ \dfrac{1}{3} \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right) \right]_0^{\infty}$

$I = \dfrac{2}{3} \left( \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 \right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\int_a^b(x^2 - x)\, dx = 18, \int_a^b x^3\, dx = 0$, then $a + b$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given $\int_a^b x^3 \, dx = 0$

$\Rightarrow \left[ \dfrac{x^4}{4} \right]_a^b = 0$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{b^4 - a^4}{4} = 0$

$\Rightarrow b^4 = a^4$

$\Rightarrow b = a$ or $b = -a$

If $b = a$, then $\int_a^b (x^2 - x) \, dx = 0$, which contradicts the given condition $\int_a^b (x^2 - x) \, dx = 18$.

Therefore, $b = -a$.

This directly gives $a + b = 0$.

To find the exact values, substituting $b = -a$ into the first integral:

$\int_a^{-a} (x^2 - x) \, dx = 18$

$\Rightarrow -\int_{-a}^a (x^2 - x) \, dx = 18$

Using properties of definite integrals for even and odd functions:

$- \left( 2 \int_0^a x^2 \, dx - 0 \right) = 18$

$\Rightarrow -2 \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^a = 18$

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{2a^3}{3} = 18$

$\Rightarrow a^3 = -27 \Rightarrow a = -3$

Since $b = -a$, we get $b = 3$.

Hence, $a + b = -3 + 3 = 0$.

Answer: $0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The function $f(x) = \int_0^x\dfrac{dt}{1 + \cos t}$ satisfies which of the following differential equations?
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = \int_0^x \dfrac{dt}{1 + \cos t}$

Using the half-angle formula $1 + \cos t = 2 \cos^2(t/2)$, we get:

$f(x) = \int_0^x \dfrac{dt}{2 \cos^2(t/2)} = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_0^x \sec^2(t/2) dt$

Integrating, we obtain:

$f(x) = \left[ \tan(t/2) \right]_0^x = \tan(x/2)$

Differentiating $f(x)$ with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{df}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2} \sec^2(x/2)$

Using the identity $\sec^2(x/2) = 1 + \tan^2(x/2)$:

$\dfrac{df}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(1 + \tan^2(x/2) \right)$

Substituting $f(x) = \tan(x/2)$:

$\dfrac{df}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left( 1 + [f(x)]^2 \right)$

$2\dfrac{df}{dx} = 1 + [f(x)]^2$

Let $I = \int_0^\pi \dfrac{1}{1 + 2^{\cos x}} \, dx$

Using the property $\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = \int_0^a f(a-x) \, dx$, we get:

$I = \int_0^\pi \dfrac{1}{1 + 2^{\cos(\pi - x)}} \, dx$

$I = \int_0^\pi \dfrac{1}{1 + 2^{-\cos x}} \, dx$

$I = \int_0^\pi \dfrac{2^{\cos x}}{2^{\cos x} + 1} \, dx$

Adding the two equations for $I$:

$2I = \int_0^\pi \left( \dfrac{1}{1 + 2^{\cos x}} + \dfrac{2^{\cos x}}{1 + 2^{\cos x}} \right) \, dx$

$2I = \int_0^\pi 1 \, dx$

$2I = \pi$

$I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{2x(1 + \sin x)}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$ is...
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{2x(1 + \sin x)}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$

Splitting the integral, we get:

$I = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{2x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx + \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\dfrac{2x \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$

The first integral is zero because the integrand $f(x) = \dfrac{2x}{1 + \cos^2 x}$ is an odd function.

The second integral has an even integrand, so:

$I = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{2x \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx = 4 \int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{x \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$

Using the property $\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx$, we get:

$I = 4 \int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{(\pi - x) \sin(\pi - x)}{1 + \cos^2(\pi - x)}dx = 4 \int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{(\pi - x) \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$

Adding the two expressions for $I$:

$2I = 4 \int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$

$I = 2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}dx$

Substituting $\cos x = t$, we get $-\sin x dx = dt$. The limits change from $1$ to $-1$:

$I = 2\pi \int_{1}^{-1}\dfrac{-dt}{1 + t^2} = 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2}$

$I = 2\pi [\tan^{-1} t]_{-1}^{1} = 2\pi \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} -\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)

$I = $2\pi \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \pi^2$

Answer: \pi^2

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of integral $\int_0^1\cot^{-1}(1 + x^2 - x)\,dx$ is...
questions.solution:
$I = \int_0^1 \cot^{-1}(1 + x^2 - x) \, dx$

$I = \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{1 + x(x - 1)}\right) \, dx$

$I = \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x - (x - 1)}{1 + x(x - 1)}\right) \, dx$

$I = \int_0^1 (\tan^{-1}x - \tan^{-1}(x - 1)) \, dx$

Using the property $\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = \int_0^a f(a - x) \, dx$ on the second term:

$\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}(x - 1) \, dx = \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}(1 - x - 1) \, dx = \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}(-x) \, dx = -\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x \, dx$

$I = \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x \, dx - \left(-\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x \, dx\right) = 2\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x \, dx$

Using integration by parts:

$I = 2 \left[ x \tan^{-1}x \right]_0^1 - 2 \int_0^1 \dfrac{x}{1 + x^2} \, dx$

$I = 2 \left( 1 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4} - 0 \right) - \left[ \log(1 + x^2) \right]_0^1$

$I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \log 2$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \log 2$

questions.solution:
Let $e^x - 1 = t^2$. Differentiating both sides, we get $e^x dx = 2t dt$.

When $x = 0$, $t^2 = e^0 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0$.

When $x = \log 5$, $t^2 = e^{\log 5} - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4 \Rightarrow t = 2$.

The denominator becomes $e^x + 3 = (t^2 + 1) + 3 = t^2 + 4$.

Substituting these into the integral, we get:

$\displaystyle\int_0^{\log 5} \dfrac{\sqrt{e^x - 1}}{e^x + 3} (e^x dx) = \int_0^2 \dfrac{t}{t^2 + 4} (2t dt)$

$= \displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{2t^2}{t^2 + 4} dt$

$= 2 \displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{t^2 + 4 - 4}{t^2 + 4} dt$

$= 2 \displaystyle\int_0^2 \left( 1 - \dfrac{4}{t^2 + 4} \right) dt$

$= 2 \left[ t - 4 \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \tan^{-1} \left( \dfrac{t}{2} \right) \right) \right]_0^2$

Using the definite integral property $\int_a^{b} f(x)dx = \int_a^{b} f(a+b-x)dx$, we substitute $x$ with $\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} - x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$:

$I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\cos(\pi/2 - x)}{1+\sin(\pi/2 - x) + \cos(\pi/2 - x)}dx$

$I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x + \sin x}dx$

Adding the two expressions for $I$:

$2I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x + \cos x}{1+\sin x + \cos x}dx$

$2I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1+\sin x + \cos x - 1}{1+\sin x + \cos x}dx$

$2I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1+\sin x + \cos x}\right)dx$

$2I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} 1 dx - \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{1+\sin x + \cos x}dx$

$2I = [x]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} - \log 2$

$2I = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - \log 2$

$2I = \dfrac{\pi}{6} - \log 2$

questions.q: If $\int_0^a (x^2 - 4x + 1)dx = 6$, then the real value of $a$ is
questions.solution:
Evaluating the given definite integral:

$\int_0^a (x^2 - 4x + 1)dx = \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} - 2x^2 + x \right]_0^a$

Substituting the limits, we get:

$\dfrac{a^3}{3} - 2a^2 + a = 6$

Multiplying by $3$ on both sides:

$a^3 - 6a^2 + 3a - 18 = 0$

Factorizing the polynomial:

$a^2(a - 6) + 3(a - 6) = 0$

$(a^2 + 3)(a - 6) = 0$

Since $a$ is a real number, $a^2 + 3 \neq 0$.

Therefore, $a - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow a = 6$.

Answer: $6$

questions.q: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{(2x^9 + 3x^8 - 5x^7 + 9x^6 + 4x^3 - x + 3)}{x^2 + 3} \, dx$ is
questions.solution:
Let the given integral be $I$. We can split the integrand into odd and even functions:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{2x^9 - 5x^7 + 4x^3 - x}{x^2 + 3} \, dx + \displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3x^8 + 9x^6 + 3}{x^2 + 3} \, dx$

The first integral is $0$ because the integrand is an odd function and the limits are symmetric about the origin.

For the second integral, simplifying the integrand gives:

$I = \displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3x^6(x^2 + 3) + 3}{x^2 + 3} \, dx = \displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left( 3x^6 + \dfrac{3}{x^2 + 3} \right) \, dx$

Since the integrand is an even function, we can write:

$I = 2 \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} \left( 3x^6 + \dfrac{3}{x^2 + 3} \right) \, dx$

Integrating with respect to $x$:

$I = 2 \left[ \dfrac{3x^7}{7} + \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \right]_0^{\sqrt{3}}$

Substituting the limits:

$I = 2 \left( \dfrac{3(\sqrt{3})^7}{7} + \sqrt{3} \tan^{-1}(1) - 0 \right)$

Using $(\sqrt{3})^7 = 27\sqrt{3}$ and $\tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$I = 2 \left( \dfrac{3 \times 27\sqrt{3}}{7} + \sqrt{3} \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)$

$I = \dfrac{162\sqrt{3}}{7} + \sqrt{3} \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{162\sqrt{3}}{7} + \sqrt{3} \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.q: The value of $\int_0^\pi\left|\sin ^3 x\right| \mathrm{d} x$ is
questions.solution:
To evaluate $\int_0^\pi\left|\sin ^3 x\right| \ dx$, note that $\sin x \geq 0$ for $x \in [0, \pi]$, so the absolute value may be removed without changing the integral.

The integral becomes $\int_0^\pi \sin^3 x \ dx$, which is separable by writing $\sin^3 x = \sin x (1 - \cos^2 x)$ using the identity $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$.

Substituting $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x \ dx$, with limits $u=1$ when $x=0$ and $u=-1$ when $x=\pi$, the integral becomes $\int_1^{-1} (1 - u^2)(-\ du) = \int_{-1}^1 (1 - u^2) \ du$.

Exploiting the evenness of $1 - u^2$ on the symmetric interval $[-1,1]$, the integral is $2\int_0^1 (1 - u^2) \ du = 2\left[u - \frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = 2(1 - \frac{1}{3}) = \frac{4}{3}$.

The value of the integral is $\frac{4}{3}$, corresponding to choice $\boxed{C}$.

Choosing $u = \log(x+1)$ and $dv = dx$ gives $du = \frac{1}{x+1} dx$ and $v = x$. Applying the formula yields:

The boundary term simplifies entirely to $\log 2$. The remaining integral is simplified by writing the integrand as $1 - \frac{1}{x+1}$, leading to:

Combining both results:

$\int_0^1 \log (x+1) \, dx = \log 2 - (1 - \log 2) = 2\log 2 - 1$.

This corresponds to option D.

questions.solution:
Given the definite integral $I = \int_2^3 x f(x) dx$ with the conditions $f(5-x)=f(x)$ and $\int_2^3 f(x) dx=2$, apply the substitution property $\int_a^b g(x) dx = \int_a^b g(a+b-x) dx$.

Since $a=2$ and $b=3$, then $a+b=5$ and $I = \int_2^3 (5-x) f(5-x) dx$.
Using the given symmetry $f(5-x)=f(x)$, this becomes $I = \int_2^3 (5-x) f(x) dx$.

Expanding the integrand: $I = 5\int_2^3 f(x) dx - \int_2^3 x f(x) dx$.
The first term is $5 \cdot 2 = 10$ by the given integral value, and the second term is $I$.

The integrand $x\left|x-\frac{1}{2}\right|$ has a discontinuity in its derivative at $x = \frac{1}{2}$, requiring integration over two intervals.

For $x \lt \frac{1}{2}$, $\left|x-\frac{1}{2}\right| = \frac{1}{2} - x$. For $x \geq \frac{1}{2}$, $\left|x-\frac{1}{2}\right| = x - \frac{1}{2}$. The integral splits accordingly:

$\int_0^1 x\left|x-\frac{1}{2}\right| dx = \int_0^{1/2} x\left(\frac{1}{2} - x\right) dx + \int_{1/2}^1 x\left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right) dx$

The first integral evaluates as:

$\int_0^{1/2} \left(\frac{x}{2} - x^2\right) dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{4} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/2} = \frac{1}{16} - \frac{1}{24} = \frac{1}{48}$

The second integral yields:

$\int_{1/2}^1 \left(x^2 - \frac{x}{2}\right) dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^2}{4}\right]_{1/2}^1 = \left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right) - \left(\frac{1}{24} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{48} = \frac{5}{48}$

Summing both parts gives $\frac{1}{48} + \frac{5}{48} = \frac{6}{48} = \frac{1}{8}$.

Final result: $\boxed{\frac{1}{8}}$

To evaluate $\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx$, apply integration by parts with $u = \tan^{-1} x$ and $dv = dx$. Differentiate to find $du = \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx$ and integrate to get $v = x$.

Applying the integration by parts formula yields $\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx = [x \tan^{-1} x]_0^1 - \int_0^1 \frac{x}{1+x^2} dx$. The boundary term evaluates to $[x \tan^{-1} x]_0^1 = (1 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4}) - (0 \cdot 0) = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

The remaining integral simplifies through substitution. Let $t = 1 + x^2$, so $dt = 2x dx$ and $x dx = \frac{1}{2} dt$. When $x = 0$, $t = 1$; at $x = 1$, $t = 2$. The integral becomes $\frac{1}{2} \int_1^2 \frac{1}{t} dt = \frac{1}{2} [\log t]_1^2 = \frac{1}{2} \log 2$.

Combining results gives $\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \log 2$, which is equivalent to $\frac{\pi}{4} - \log \sqrt{2}$.

The expression matches option B.

Consider the integral $I = \int_{1/2}^2 \frac{1}{x} \csc^{101}\left(x - \frac{1}{x}\right) dx$.

Applying the substitution $x = 1/t$ yields $dx = -1/t^2 dt$, with limits transforming as $x = 1/2 \Rightarrow t = 2$ and $x = 2 \Rightarrow t = 1/2$.

The integrand transforms as follows: $1/x \rightarrow t$, and $x - 1/x \rightarrow 1/t - t = -(t - 1/t)$. Since $\csc(-\theta) = -\csc\theta$ and the exponent is odd, $\csc^{101}(-(t-1/t)) = -\csc^{101}(t-1/t)$.

Substituting gives:

$I = \int_2^{1/2} t \cdot (-\csc^{101}(t-1/t)) \cdot (-1/t^2) dt = \int_2^{1/2} \frac{1}{t} \csc^{101}\left(t-\frac{1}{t}\right) dt$

Reversing the limits introduces a sign change:

$I = -\int_{1/2}^2 \frac{1}{t} \csc^{101}\left(t-\frac{1}{t}\right) dt$

Since the variable of integration is a dummy variable, we recognize this as $-I$, leading to $I = -I \Rightarrow 2I = 0 \Rightarrow I = 0$.

The value of the integral is $\boxed{A}$.

questions.solution:
Continuity requires $\lim_{x \to 3} g(x) = g(3)$, so $K = \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{\int_3^{f(x)} 3t^2\,dt}{x-3}$.

The limit is indeterminate ($0/0$), so apply L'Hôpital's Rule. Differentiate numerator and denominator separately.

Denominator derivative: $\frac{d}{dx}(x-3) = 1$.

Numerator derivative (via Leibniz rule): $\frac{d}{dx} \int_3^{f(x)} 3t^2\,dt = 3(f(x))^2 f'(x)$.

$K = \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{3(f(x))^2 f'(x)}{1} = 3(f(3))^2 f'(3)$.

Given $f(3)=3$ and $f'(3)=\frac{1}{27}$, so $K = 3 \cdot 9 \cdot \frac{1}{27} = 1$.

$\boxed{1}$

Given integral: $I = \int_1^3 \frac{\log x^2}{\log (16 x^2 - 8 x^3 + x^4)} \, dx$

Simplify the integrand. The numerator is $\log x^2 = 2 \log x$.
The denominator’s argument factors as $16x^2 - 8x^3 + x^4 = x^2(16 - 8x + x^2) = x^2(x - 4)^2$, so $\log(x^2(x - 4)^2) = 2 \log x + 2 \log |x - 4|$.
Since $x \in [1,3]$, $x - 4 < 0$, yielding $|x - 4| = 4 - x$.

Substituting, $I = \int_1^3 \frac{2 \log x}{2 \log x + 2 \log(4 - x)} \, dx = \int_1^3 \frac{\log x}{\log x + \log(4 - x)} \, dx$.

Apply the substitution $x \mapsto 4 - x$ to the integral, giving:
$I = \int_1^3 \frac{\log(4 - x)}{\log(4 - x) + \log x} \, dx$.

Adding these two expressions for $I$:
$2I = \int_1^3 \left( \frac{\log x}{\log x + \log(4 - x)} + \frac{\log(4 - x)}{\log(4 - x) + \log x} \right) dx = \int_1^3 \frac{\log x + \log(4 - x)}{\log x + \log(4 - x)} \, dx = \int_1^3 1 \, dx$.

Thus, $2I = [x]_1^3 = 2$, so $I = 1$.

$\boxed{1}$

Applying the substitution property $\int_a^b f(x) \, \mathrm{d}x = \int_a^b f(a+b-x) \, \mathrm{d}x$ with $a=0$, $b=1$ yields $I = \int_0^1 \log \left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right) \, \mathrm{d}x$.

questions.solution:
The integral $I = \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2) dx$ can be evaluated using trigonometric identities and substitution techniques.

Since $1-x+x^2 = \left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3}{4} \gt 0$ for $x \in [0,1]$, the identity $\tan^{-1} A + \tan^{-1} \frac{1}{A} = \frac{\pi}{2}$ applies, giving $\tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2) = \frac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1} \left(\frac{1}{1-x+x^2}\right).

Substituting yields $I = \int_0^1 $\frac{\pi}{2}$dx - \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}$\left(\frac{1}{1-x+x^2}\right)$dx = $\frac{\pi}{2} - \int_$0^1 \tan^{-1}$\left(\frac{1}{1-x+x^2}\right)$dx$.

Using the identity $\tan^{-1} x - \tan^{-1} (x-1) = \tan^{-1} $\left(\frac{1}{1-x+x^2}\right)$, the integral becomes $I = \frac{\pi}{2} - \int_0^1 (\tan^{-1} x - \tan^{-1} (x-1)) dx$.

Substituting $u = x-1$ in the second term gives $\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} (x-1) dx = \int_{-1}^0 \tan^{-1} u du = -\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} u du$ by odd symmetry.

Thus, $I = \frac{\pi}{2} - \left(\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx + \int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} - 2\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx$.

Integration by parts with $v = \tan^{-1} x$, $du = dx$ yields $\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx = [x \tan^{-1} x]_0^1 - \int_0^1 \frac{x}{1+x^2} dx = \frac{\pi}{4} - \int_0^1 \frac{x}{1+x^2} dx$.

The remaining integral evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}\log 2$ via substitution $t = 1+x^2$, giving $\int_0^1 \tan^{-1} x dx = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\log 2$.

Substituting back, $I = \frac{\pi}{2} - 2\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\log 2\right) = \log 2$.

Final answer: $\log 2$

Evaluate the integral: $I = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} (\sqrt{\tan x} + \sqrt{\cot x}) \, \mathrm{d}x$

Begin by simplifying the integrand:

$\sqrt{\tan x} + \sqrt{\cot x} = \frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\cos x}} + \frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sqrt{\sin x}} = \frac{\sin x + \cos x}{\sqrt{\sin x \cos x}}$

The integral becomes:

$I = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sin x + \cos x}{\sqrt{\sin x \cos x}} \, \mathrm{d}x$

Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{2}$ and recognize that $2\sin x \cos x = \sin 2x$:

$I = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sqrt{2}(\sin x + \cos x)}{\sqrt{\sin 2x}} \, \mathrm{d}x$

Use the substitution $t = \sin x - \cos x$, giving $\mathrm{d}t = (\cos x + \sin x) \, \mathrm{d}x$.
Then $t^2 = 1 - 2\sin x \cos x$, so $\sin x \cos x = \frac{1 - t^2}{2}$.

When $x = 0$, $t = -1$; when $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$, $t = 0$. Substituting:

$I = \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\sqrt{(1 - t^2)/2}} = \sqrt{2} \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}} \, \mathrm{d}t$

The antiderivative is $\arcsin t$, so:

$I = \sqrt{2} [\arcsin t]_{-1}^{0} = \sqrt{2} (\arcsin 0 - \arcsin(-1)) = \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)

The final result is $I = $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}.$$

Given the integral $I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \frac{x}{1+\sin x} \, dx$, apply the transformation property $\int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_a^b f(a+b-x) \, dx$ with $a+b = \pi$:

$I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \frac{\pi-x}{1+\sin x} \, dx$

Adding this to the original expression yields:

$2I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \frac{\pi}{1+\sin x} \, dx$

Rewriting the integrand through rationalization:

$\frac{1}{1+\sin x} = \frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x - \sec x \tan x$

Integration gives:

$\int \left(\sec^2 x - \sec x \tan x\right) \, dx = \tan x - \sec x + C$

Evaluating the definite integral:

$2I = \pi \left[ \tan x - \sec x \right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}$

$\tan\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) - \sec\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\sqrt{3} - (-2) = 2-\sqrt{3}$
$\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) - \sec\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3} - 2$

$2I = \pi \left[ (2-\sqrt{3}) - (\sqrt{3}-2) \right] = \pi(4 - 2\sqrt{3}) = 2\pi(2-\sqrt{3})$

Thus $I = \pi(2-\sqrt{3})$, which corresponds to option B.

$I = \int_0^2 \frac{3x}{x^2+4} dx + \int_0^2 \frac{1}{x^2+4} dx$

For the first term, substitute $u = x^2 + 4$ so that $du = 2x dx$ and $x dx = \frac{1}{2} du$:
When $x = 0$, $u = 4$
When $x = 2$, $u = 8$
This yields $\frac{3}{2} \int_4^8 \frac{1}{u} du = \frac{3}{2} \ln\left|u\right| \Big|_4^8 = \frac{3}{2} (\ln 8 - \ln 4) = \frac{3}{2} \ln 2 = \ln(2\sqrt{2})$

The second term follows the standard form:
$\int_0^2 \frac{1}{x^2+4} dx = \frac{1}{2} \arctan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) \Big|_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - 0\right) = \frac{\pi}{8}$

The complete integral evaluates to $\ln(2\sqrt{2}) + \frac{\pi}{8}$, matching option C.

Using the identity for inverse tangents, $\tan^{-1}(y) + \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{1}{y} \right) = \frac{\pi}{2}$ when $y > 0$ and $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ when $y < 0$.

Let $y = \frac{x}{x^{2} + 1}$. Since $x^{2} + 1 > 0$ for all real $x$, the sign of $y$ matches that of $x$.

For $x \in (0, 3]$, $y > 0$, so the integrand equals $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

For $x \in [-1, 0)$, $y < 0$, so the integrand equals $-\frac{\pi}{2}$.

Splitting the integral at $x = 0$ gives:
$I = \int_{-1}^{0} -\frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{3} \frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{d}x = -\frac{\pi}{2}(0 - (-1)) + \frac{\pi}{2}(3 - 0) = -\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{3\pi}{2} = \pi$.

The final result is $\pi$.

questions.q: The value of $\int_0^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x$ is (where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer function not greater than $x$ )
questions.solution:
To evaluate the integral $\int_0^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x$, split the integration interval where the greatest integer function $\left[x^2\right]$ changes value. The critical points occur at $x$ values where $x^2$ is an integer between $0 and 4$: $x = 0$, $1$, $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, and $2$.

Break the integral into subintervals based on the behavior of $\left[x^2\right]$:

$\int_0^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x = \int_0^1\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x + \int_1^{\sqrt{2}}\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x + \int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}}\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x + \int_{\sqrt{3}}^{2}\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x$

On $[0,1)$, $0 \le x^2 \lt 1$ so $\left[x^2\right] = 0$. On $[1,\sqrt{2})$, $1 \le x^2 \lt 2$ so $\left[x^2\right] = 1$. On $[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$, $2 \le x^2 \lt 3$ so $\left[x^2\right] = 2$. On $[\sqrt{3},2]$, $3 \le x^2 \lt 4$ so $\left[x^2\right] = 3$.

Substitute the constant values:

$\int_0^2\left[x^2\right] \mathrm{d} x = \int_0^1 0 \mathrm{d} x + \int_1^{\sqrt{2}} 1 \mathrm{d} x + \int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}} 2 \mathrm{d} x + \int_{\sqrt{3}}^{2} 3 \mathrm{d} x$

Evaluate each integral:

$\int_0^1 0 \mathrm{d} x = 0$
$\int_1^{\sqrt{2}} 1 \mathrm{d} x = \sqrt{2} - 1$
$\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{3}} 2 \mathrm{d} x = 2(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}) = 2\sqrt{3} - 2\sqrt{2}$
$\int_{\sqrt{3}}^{2} 3 \mathrm{d} x = 3(2 - \sqrt{3}) = 6 - 3\sqrt{3}$

Sum the results:

$0 + (\sqrt{2} - 1) + (2\sqrt{3} - 2\sqrt{2}) + (6 - 3\sqrt{3}) = 5 - \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$

The result corresponds to option A.

The integral splits into two parts:
$\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^2 - x - 2)dx + \int_{-1}^{2}(-x^2 + x + 2)dx$

Evaluating the first integral:
$\left[\frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^2}{2} - 2x\right]_{-2}^{-1} = \frac{11}{6}$

Evaluating the second integral:
$\left[-\frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^2}{2} + 2x\right]_{-1}^{2} = \frac{9}{2}$

The total integral is $\frac{11}{6} + \frac{9}{2} = \frac{19}{3}$.

Final answer: $\frac{19}{3}$

questions.solution:
Evaluating the integral $\int_1^4 \log [x] dx$ requires handling the greatest integer function $[x]$ by partitioning the domain where $[x]$ remains constant—specifically at integer boundaries.

Between $x = 1$ and $x = 4$, the integral splits into three parts:
$\int_1^4 \log [x] dx = \int_1^2 \log 1 dx + \int_2^3 \log 2 dx + \int_3^4 \log 3 dx$.

The first integral vanishes because $\log 1 = 0$. The second evaluates to $\log 2 \cdot (3-2) = \log 2$, while the third gives $\log 3 \cdot (4-3) = \log 3$.

Adding these yields $\log 2 + \log 3 = \log (2 \cdot 3) = \log 6$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.solution: $Let \begin{aligned} I=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{\cos 3 x+1}{2 \cos x-1} d x \\ &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{\cos 3 x-\cos \frac{3 \pi}{3}}{2\left(\cos x-\cos \frac{\pi}{3}\right)} d x \\=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{\left(4 \cos ^{3} x-3 \cos x\right)-\left(4 \cos ^{3} \frac{\pi}{3}-3 \cos \frac{\pi}{3}\right)}{2\left(\cos x-\cos \frac{\pi}{3}\right)} d x \\=& 2 \int_{0}^{\pi / 2}\left(\frac{\cos ^{3} x-\cos ^{3} \frac{\pi}{3}}{\cos x-\cos \frac{\pi}{3}}\right) d x \\=\frac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi / 2}\left(\frac{\cos x-\cos \frac{\pi}{3}}{\cos x-\cos \frac{\pi}{3}}\right) d x \\=& \int_{0}^{\pi / 2}\left(1+\cos 2 x+\frac{1}{2}+\cos x\right) d x-\frac{3 \pi}{4} \\=& \frac{3 \pi}{4}+1-\frac{3 \pi}{4}=1 \end{aligned}$
